source.title: eGAD! double descent is explained by Generalized Aliasing Decomposition
source.authors: M. Transtrum; G. Hart; Tyler J. Jarvis; J. Whitehead

record.tranche_reason: The paper presents its own analyses of model-size risk curves and argues that generalized aliasing, rather than a bias–variance account, explains double and multiple descent. It also identifies settings where the generic curve changes or does not appear.
record.gate_note: The paper reports risk curves for random-feature models, Fourier fitting, differential-equation collocation, and cluster expansion. Figure 8 varies training-point count but reports aliasing-operator norm rather than test risk, so it does not test whether more samples raise test error. The paper does not sweep training epochs. Results cited from other work were not extracted.
record.test_reason: The paper reports its own model-size risk curves for random-feature, Fourier, collocation and cluster-expansion regression. It argues that a generalized aliasing decomposition explains double and multiple descent, and shows settings where the second descent is missing or the interpolation threshold plays no role.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors argue random-feature models do best in the overparameterized regime, while physics-ordered models do best in the classical regime. In their cluster-expansion example the classical sweet spot beat the large-model limit.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes linear regression and related structured fitting problems using a generalized aliasing decomposition; its random neural-feature examples use fixed random features rather than the original deep-network training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk curves change with basis choice and ordering, training-point placement or perturbation, and regularization strength. The paper contrasts random and natural ordering and uniform and perturbed collocation points.

fits_no_version.finding: Aliasing-operator norm versus number of training points for a Legendre basis: random points give far larger ‖A‖ than Legendre–Gauss points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-point placement controls the aliasing magnitude and hence the size of the risk peak.

record.problems: Most plotted risk outcomes are qualitative figure-based curves without numerical risk values or uncertainty estimates. The neural-network examples are random-feature models, not end-to-end trained deep networks. Epoch-wise double descent and test-risk changes from increasing sample count are not tested.
record.rows_left_out: No separate risk rows were extracted for cubic-spline and high-order-spline collocation because the text does not describe their risk-curve shapes; the plotted risk values alone are figure-only. Figure 8 varies training-point count but reports aliasing norm, not risk. Other plotted GAD components are not themselves test-risk outcomes.

untested.parts: No deep networks trained end-to-end; only fixed random-feature regressions.
Figure 8 varies the training-set size but reports aliasing norm, not test risk.
No single complexity measure is tested across axes.
No label-noise sweep; no empirical test of optimally tuned regularization.

missing.what: Naturally ordered cluster expansion reaches a lower optimal risk, at a classical sweet spot, than randomly ordered cluster expansion does in its large-model limit.
missing.locator: Section III D, final paragraph; Figure 7

missing.what: Risk curves for cubic-spline and order-65 spline collocation bases are plotted but their shapes are not described in the text.

record.verdict_notes: The V1 links were removed because the random-feature models are not trained deep networks. Removing them also removes the V1 verdict. All risk evidence is figure-only, with no numbers or uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: Conventional deep networks trained end-to-end are not evaluated; the neural-network examples are two-layer random-feature models with random features.
No risk curve over training epochs is reported.
The paper does not report test risk increasing when training sample count increases near the interpolation threshold.
The demonstrated classes are the paper's regression, signal-processing, differential-equation, and materials examples; the paper does not establish the result for all model classes.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper does not sweep label-noise levels or test optimally tuned regularization. Its regularization discussion is analytic and concerns sufficiently large ridge penalty.
The paper does not recast the second descent as an ordinary U-shaped curve by measuring complexity in effective parameters.
